title: Destructive or Advancing Operation Is the Only Way to Read State
pattern: A custom type offers only a consuming or advancing operation (`pop`, `next`, `parse_token`, `reset`/`take`) to observe a value, with no non-destructive query (`peek`, `current`, `last`, `get`) on `&self`.
why_bad: Every inspection changes state. Parsers cannot look ahead without position-restoring hacks, callers who want to examine the top of a stack must pop and push back, and metrics can only be read by resetting them, so two readers (a dashboard and an alert) corrupt each other's counts.
detection: A type's public API where each accessor for some piece of state takes `&mut self` and removes, advances past or resets that state, and no `&self` method returns the same value; include `reset_*`/`take_*` methods that return the previous value when no plain getter exists.
counterexample: Types where a non-destructive read is impossible or unsafe: channels, sockets, one-shot readers, concurrent queues where a separate peek would race with other consumers, and atomic snapshot-and-reset primitives used for interval metrics. Types that already offer the read side (`Vec::last`, `Iterator::peekable`, a separate getter).
source: Michael Feathers, *Working Effectively with Legacy Code* (2004), Ch. 14; Erich Gamma et al., *Design Patterns* (1994), "Iterator"; Steve McConnell, *Code Complete* (2004), Ch. 18; Richard L. Sites, *Understanding Software Dynamics* (2021), Ch. 5.
